vignette:
# Takeshi

Takeshi Yamamoto was forty-eight when the truck hit him. He'd been driving home from the fabrication shop on a Wednesday evening in late October, his hands still carrying the smell of welding flux and hot steel. The intersection at Maple and Fifth was unremarkable—he'd driven through it a thousand times—but this time a sedan ran the red light at full speed. The collision came from his passenger side, a sickening crunch of metal that folded the car inward like paper. His left shoulder and ribs took the force of impact; his body slammed sideways against the driver's door, his head whipping against the window. For a moment there was only noise—the shriek of tearing metal, the hiss of steam, his own ragged breathing—and then a profound, terrifying silence. When the paramedics extracted him, he could not feel his left arm.

The physical injuries healed. Takeshi spent three months in rehabilitation, regaining strength and sensation in his shoulder. The orthopedic surgeon cleared him to return to welding by early spring. But something had broken that did not show on X-rays. Within weeks of resuming work, Takeshi found himself gripped by a terror he could not quite name. His body had become a recording device of the collision itself. When memories of the crash surfaced—and they came without warning, triggered by the smallest sensory fragments—his left shoulder and ribs would seize with the same sharp, crushing pain he'd felt in those first seconds after impact. His entire body would lock into the exact twisted position he'd been in during the collision, muscles rigid and trembling. The pain was not metaphorical; it was vivid and unmistakable, as though his nervous system had encoded the accident so completely that recalling it meant reliving it in full sensory detail. Every time the memory returned, it came not as a thought but as a complete takeover—the sound of the impact, the smell of coolant and gasoline, the taste of blood in his mouth, the pressure of the door frame against his ribs—all of it flooding back at once, indistinguishable from the original event.

This flooding of memory had a cruel consequence. Takeshi began to notice that certain triggers in his everyday world would reliably summon the crash back into his body. The sight of a car accident on the news, or worse, seeing another vehicle struck in traffic, would immediately pull the memory forward with violent intensity. The smell of alcohol—someone's whiskey breath on the bus, the faint reek of beer from a passing bar—would trigger the cascade, because the driver who hit him had been drunk, and that smell had been present in the wreckage. But most insidious were the sounds: the sharp honk of a horn, the screech of tires, even just the particular metallic rattle of a heavy truck passing on the street outside the fabrication shop where he worked. Each sound was a doorway back into that twisted position, back into the crushing pain in his shoulder, back into the sensory totality of the collision itself.

By autumn of the following year, Takeshi's life had contracted around these connections. He began leaving the shop early on days when heavy traffic passed nearby, unable to tolerate the sounds that reliably dragged him back into his body's memory of trauma. His wife, Keiko, noticed him flinching at ordinary car sounds, saw him grip the armrest of the passenger seat with white knuckles whenever she drove. He had stopped going to the markets he and Keiko once visited together on Saturday mornings, because the parking lots were full of moving vehicles and near-misses that kept triggering the vivid, sensory re-living of the crash. The memory had become so convincing in its totality—so completely real across every sense—that Takeshi had come to believe his body was not safe in the world, that the accident was always one sound, one smell, one glimpse of a collision away from happening again. He was fifty-one now, and he had come to see himself as a man whose nervous system had been permanently rewired by trauma, a man whose own body had become the enemy. It was only when Keiko insisted, with a firmness born of months of watching him disappear, that he finally made an appointment with a trauma therapist.
